facts_summary: Dispute over partition of suit properties between children of the deceased's first wife and his second wife. The second wife got revenue records mutated in her and her son's names and denied the first wife's children joint possession, contending that the first wife was never lawfully married to the deceased. The trial court and High Court relied on oral testimony and long continuous cohabitation to uphold the marriage and decreed partition.
legal_issues: Whether continuous cohabitation and recognition in the community creates a strong legal presumption of marriage under Section 50 of the Evidence Act in the absence of documentary proof.
Whether children born of such union are legitimate and entitled to partition and inheritance in ancestral and separate properties.
decision_holding: Appeal dismissed. The Supreme Court upheld the preliminary decree for partition, holding that continuous cohabitation established a valid presumption of marriage.
legal_principles: Law strongly presumes in favor of marriage and against concubinage when a man and woman cohabit continuously as husband and wife and are treated as such by society. Such presumption can only be displaced by heavy, incontrovertible evidence. Children of such unions inherit under personal succession law.
sub_case_type: Marriage Validity / Presumption of Marriage & Succession
relevance_reason: Substantively adjudicates presumption of marriage and succession entitlements of children in partition of joint property.

case_name: Geeta @ Reeta Mishra v. Ajay Kumar Mishra
candidate_laws: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
facts_summary: Matrimonial dispute involving multiple cross-petitions for divorce, restitution, maintenance under Section 24 HMA, and domestic violence complaints. The parties lived separately for over 15 years with complete breakdown of ties. High Court refused divorce.
legal_issues: Whether protracted separation and irreconcilable differences justify dissolution of marriage under Article 142 on ground of irretrievable breakdown.
Determination of adequate permanent alimony under Section 25 HMA.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. Supreme Court granted a decree of divorce dissolving the marriage under Article 142, and directed the husband to pay Rs. 25 Lakhs as permanent alimony, quashing all allied proceedings.
legal_principles: In long-standing matrimonial deadlocks where emotional connection is irretrievably lost, continuing the legal status of marriage serves no social purpose. The Court will exercise Article 142 to decree divorce while ensuring just and equitable permanent alimony.
relevance_reason: Directly dissolves marriage and awards permanent alimony under HMA and Article 142.

case_name: Komal Krishan Arora & Ors. v. Sandeep Kumar & Ors.
facts_summary: Dispute between separated parents over the custody and guardianship of their minor daughter. The mother resided in the UK and sought permanent custody, while the father and paternal grandparents had physical custody in India. Family Court and High Court passed conflicting orders regarding custody and passport release.
legal_issues: Custody and guardianship of a minor child under Section 26 HMA and Guardians and Wards Act, 1890.
Welfare of the minor child when custodial parent plans relocation abroad versus continuity of environment in India.
decision_holding: Appeals disposed of. Custody arrangements structured to ensure primary custody with the mother while protecting meaningful physical visitation and video access for the father and grandparents.
legal_principles: In child custody disputes under GWA and Section 26 HMA, neither parent possesses an absolute legal right. The paramount consideration is the comprehensive physical, psychological, educational, and emotional welfare of the minor child.
relevance_reason: Core child custody and guardianship adjudication under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 and Section 26 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

case_name: Amanjot Singh Chadha v. Union of India & Ors.
facts_summary: Writ petition challenging the constitutional validity of Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (Restitution of Conjugal Rights) on the ground that it violates the fundamental right to privacy, bodily autonomy, and equality under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.
legal_issues: Whether Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 providing for restitution of conjugal rights infringes the fundamental right to privacy and bodily autonomy under Article 21.
Whether statutory restitution of conjugal rights is an unconstitutional state co-option of marital cohabitation.
decision_holding: Writ petition heard and principles of constitutional scrutiny applied, upholding the statutory objective of marital reconciliation while emphasizing that courts cannot compel physical cohabitation through coercive execution.
legal_principles: Section 9 of HMA is designed to encourage reconciliation and preservation of marriage, but a decree for restitution of conjugal rights cannot be executed by physical force or coercion against the will of a spouse, respecting constitutional privacy and dignity.
sub_case_type: Constitutional Family Law / Restitution of Conjugal Rights (s.9 HMA)
relevance_reason: Directly scrutinizes the constitutional validity and operation of Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

case_name: Ivan Rathinam v. Milan Joseph
facts_summary: Respondent and his mother claimed that the appellant was the respondent's biological father, alleging an extra-marital relationship during the subsistence of the mother's valid marriage with another man ('RK'). The respondent sought maintenance and declaratory relief. The appellant denied paternity, invoking the conclusive presumption of legitimacy under Section 112 Evidence Act and res judicata.
legal_issues: Whether the conclusive presumption of legitimacy under Section 112 of the Evidence Act determines paternity in law in the absence of proof of non-access.
Whether a Family Court can reopen a maintenance petition and entertain a second round of litigation barred by res judicata.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. High Court and Family Court orders reopening proceedings were set aside; held that the respondent is conclusively presumed to be the legitimate child of 'RK' and cannot claim maintenance against the appellant.
legal_principles: Section 112 of the Evidence Act establishes that legitimacy conclusively determines paternity unless non-access between the spouses at the time of conception is proved. A child born during a valid marriage cannot claim to be the child of a third party to demand maintenance, and successive petitions are barred by res judicata.
sub_case_type: Paternity & Maintenance / Conclusive Legitimacy (s.112 Evidence Act)
relevance_reason: Directly applies Section 112 Evidence Act and Family Courts Act to determine legitimacy, paternity, and maintenance liabilities.

case_name: Vijaya Kumari S & Another v. Union of India
facts_summary: Married intending couples had commenced surrogacy procedures and frozen their embryos prior to the enforcement of the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021. The new Act imposed an upper age limit (female 50 years, male 55 years) under Section 4(iii)(c)(I), preventing the couples from completing the surrogacy process.
legal_issues: Whether the upper age-restrictions under Section 4(iii)(c)(I) of the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 apply retrospectively to couples who had frozen their embryos prior to the enforcement of the Act.
Protection of reproductive autonomy and legitimate expectations under Article 21.
decision_holding: Writ petition allowed. Held that the age restrictions cannot be applied retrospectively to disqualify couples who had already commenced the medical process and frozen embryos before the Act came into force.
legal_principles: Substantive statutory restrictions affecting reproductive rights and parenthood cannot operate retrospectively to extinguish rights where intending parents had altered their position by freezing embryos under prior medical guidelines. Article 21 encompasses reproductive autonomy.
relevance_reason: Substantively determines parenthood and family formation rights under the Surrogacy Act, interacting with marriage and adoption frameworks.

case_name: P. Anjanappa (D) By Lrs v. A.P. Nanjundappa & Ors.
facts_summary: Suit for partition and separate possession among coparceners and branches of a Joint Hindu Family. Issues arose regarding the validity and binding effect of registered release deeds executed by certain members, and whether an unregistered palupatti (partition memorandum) could be relied on for collateral purposes to establish severance of joint status.
legal_issues: Legal effect of registered release deeds on coparcenary membership and share entitlements under the Hindu Succession Act.
Admissibility of an unregistered palupatti for collateral purpose of demonstrating severance of joint family status.
Ascertainment of partitionable joint family estate and inter se shares.
decision_holding: Appeal disposed of. Shares re-determined; held that registered release deeds effectively relinquished shares, and the unregistered palupatti was admissible for the collateral purpose of establishing severance of joint status.
legal_principles: A registered release deed executed for consideration extinguishes the coparcenary share of the releasor. An unregistered partition deed or palupatti cannot effect division of immovable property by metes and bounds, but is admissible under the proviso to Section 49 Registration Act to prove severance of joint family status and separate possession.
sub_case_type: Succession & Partition / Joint Family Settlement & Palupatti
relevance_reason: Substantively interprets coparcenary rights, devolution of shares, and effect of family settlements under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.

case_name: Smt. N. Usha Rani and Anr. v. Moodudula Srinivas
facts_summary: Wife and minor child filed for maintenance under Section 125 CrPC. Family Court granted monthly maintenance. High Court reduced and partially denied maintenance to the wife accepting the husband's contention that she had left the matrimonial home without sufficient cause.
legal_issues: Whether the High Court was justified in depriving a destitute wife of maintenance under Section 125 CrPC on unsubstantiated allegations of desertion.
Assessment of maintenance quantum commensurate with the earning capacity of the husband.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. High Court order set aside and Family Court maintenance order restored in full.
legal_principles: Under Section 125 CrPC, the husband has a non-negotiable statutory obligation to maintain his wife and child. Vague pleas of desertion cannot defeat maintenance unless deliberate refusal to live together without just cause is established by clear evidence.
sub_case_type: Maintenance & Child Support (s.125 CrPC & Family Courts Act)
relevance_reason: Directly adjudicates spousal and child maintenance rights under Section 125 CrPC and the Family Courts Act, 1984.

case_name: Sau. Jiya v. Kuldeep
facts_summary: The husband was granted a decree of divorce by the Family Court under Section 13 HMA, which was affirmed by the High Court. The appellant-wife challenged the dissolution and sought substantial enhancement of permanent alimony under Section 25 HMA.
legal_issues: Determination of permanent alimony under Section 25 HMA upon grant of divorce decree.
Balancing the husband's financial liabilities in his new family against the maintenance rights of the divorced wife and child.
decision_holding: Appeal partly allowed. Decree of divorce affirmed; permanent alimony enhanced from Rs. 10 Lakhs to Rs. 20 Lakhs.
legal_principles: When awarding permanent alimony under Section 25 HMA, the court must ensure that the divorced spouse is awarded an amount sufficient to prevent destitution and maintain dignity, regardless of the husband's remarriage or secondary liabilities.
relevance_reason: Directly adjudicates permanent alimony and divorce under Sections 13 and 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

case_name: Kuldeep Singh v. The State of Punjab & Ors.
facts_summary: Appellant sought quashing of an FIR lodged by the complainant's family alleging kidnapping, rape, and intimidation. In reality, the appellant and the prosecutrix were majors who had solemnized a Hindu marriage, resided as husband and wife, and the prosecutrix affirmed the marriage in judicial proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether criminal prosecution for rape and kidnapping under IPC can continue when the parties entered into a consensual marriage solemnized under Hindu personal law.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. Criminal proceedings and FIR quashed.
legal_principles: Criminal law cannot be used by disgruntled families to weaponize rape charges against a husband when two consenting adults have solemnized a lawful marriage and lived as husband and wife.
sub_case_type: Matrimonial Criminal / Marriage & Rape FIR Quashing
relevance_reason: Quashing of criminal proceedings intersecting proof of lawful marriage under Hindu Marriage Act and consensual marital relations.

case_name: Sri Mahesh v. Sangram & Ors.
facts_summary: Dispute concerning whether an adoption made by a Hindu widow in 1969 related back to the death of her husband who died in 1952, so as to divest properties that had already vested absolutely in the widow under Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
legal_issues: Whether the Shastric doctrine of 'Relation Back' applies to adoptions made after the commencement of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956.
Whether a post-1956 adopted son can divest properties vested absolutely in an adoptive mother under Section 14(1) HSA or in third-party alienees.
decision_holding: Appeal dismissed. Held that the doctrine of relation back stands abrogated by Section 12 of HAMA; the adopted son takes rights only from the date of adoption and cannot divest properties vested prior thereto.
legal_principles: Section 12 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 completely abolished the old Hindu law doctrine of 'Relation Back'. An adoption takes effect only from the date of adoption, and the adopted child cannot divest any person (including the adoptive mother) of any estate that vested prior to the adoption.
sub_case_type: Adoption & Succession / Doctrine of Relation Back
relevance_reason: Landmark decision authoritatively interpreting Section 12 of HAMA and Section 14 HSA regarding the abolition of the doctrine of relation back.

case_name: Geddam Jhansi & Anr. v. The State of Telangana & Ors.
candidate_laws: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
facts_summary: Following matrimonial rupture, the wife lodged criminal cases under Section 498A IPC, Dowry Prohibition Act, and domestic violence proceedings roping in the married sister-in-law and brother-in-law who resided separately. High Court dismissed their Section 482 CrPC quashing petition.
legal_issues: Whether criminal prosecution and DV proceedings against distant in-laws residing separately can be quashed under Section 482 CrPC when allegations are omnibus and devoid of specific overt acts.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. Criminal proceedings and charges against the appellants (distant in-laws) were quashed.
legal_principles: Courts must prevent the roping in of distant relatives and in-laws residing in separate households on general and omnibus allegations of dowry harassment in matrimonial breakdowns.
sub_case_type: Matrimonial Criminal & DV / Quashing Against In-Laws
relevance_reason: Deals with quashing of criminal prosecution and domestic violence complaints against in-laws under Section 482 CrPC.

case_name: Sukhdev Singh v. Sukhbir Kaur
facts_summary: Husband filed a petition under Section 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 seeking a declaration that the marriage was null and void due to a pre-existing subsistence of marriage under Section 5(i). The wife applied for permanent alimony and maintenance under Section 25 HMA, which the husband resisted claiming Section 25 does not apply to a void marriage.
legal_issues: Whether a spouse of a marriage declared null and void under Section 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is entitled to claim permanent alimony and maintenance under Section 25 of the Act.
Whether Section 25 HMA applies to decrees of nullity passed under Section 11.
decision_holding: Appeal dismissed. Supreme Court held that Section 25 HMA empowers the court to grant permanent alimony even in proceedings where the marriage is declared null and void under Section 11.
legal_principles: Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 uses the term 'any decree' and applies to decrees of nullity under Section 11 as well as divorce under Section 13. A woman who was misled into or entered a void marriage is not stripped of her statutory entitlement to permanent alimony and maintenance.
relevance_reason: Landmark decision authoritatively establishing the statutory right to permanent alimony under Section 25 HMA even where marriage is declared void under Section 11.

case_name: Suman Mishra & Ors. v. The State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
facts_summary: Wife registered an FIR roping in her husband and multiple in-laws with allegations of dowry harassment under Section 498A IPC, and subsequently leveled grave allegations of attempted rape against family members. High Court refused to quash proceedings under Section 482 CrPC.
legal_issues: Abuse of process through escalating malicious allegations (attempted rape) in matrimonial disputes to harass in-laws.
Quashing of false matrimonial prosecutions under Section 482 CrPC.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. Criminal proceedings against the in-laws quashed.
legal_principles: When matrimonial discord leads to retaliatory and wildly improbable allegations of sexual offences against family members, the High Court must exercise its inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC to quash malicious prosecution.
relevance_reason: Quashing of malicious matrimonial criminal complaints under Section 482 CrPC arising from marital breakdown.

case_name: Kiran Raju Penumacha v. Tejuswini Chowdhury
facts_summary: Parties dissolved their marriage by mutual consent under Section 13-B HMA and incorporated terms regarding joint parenting and custody of their minor daughter. Subsequent disputes arose regarding international travel, schooling, and custody enforcement.
legal_issues: Enforceability and modification of custody arrangements agreed upon during mutual consent divorce under Section 13-B HMA.
Paramount welfare of child under Section 26 HMA over contractual terms in consent decrees.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed in part; matter remitted to the Family Court for fresh consideration of custody and schooling based on updated child welfare evaluation.
legal_principles: Terms agreed by parents in a consent divorce decree regarding child custody are not immutable. The welfare of the minor under Section 26 HMA is of overriding importance and can be re-evaluated whenever circumstances change.
relevance_reason: Directly adjudicates child custody modification under Section 26 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 post-mutual consent divorce.

case_name: N.P. Saseendran v. N.P. Ponnamma & Ors.
facts_summary: Dispute among family members regarding the validity and revocation of a registered gift deed executed within the family, and subsequent suit for partition of joint family properties.
legal_issues: Whether an unconditional registered gift deed of property can be unilaterally canceled or revoked by the donor.
Maintainability of partition suit regarding gifted properties.
decision_holding: Appeal dismissed. Revocation of gift deed held invalid; partition disallowed as to validly gifted property.
legal_principles: A valid gift of immovable property executed and registered under Section 123 TPA, once accepted, cannot be unilaterally revoked under Section 126 TPA without mutual agreement or fraud.
relevance_reason: Substantively determines partition rights and validity of family property transfers under succession and transfer laws.

case_name: Ramanuj Kumar v. Priyanka
facts_summary: Husband filed for divorce on grounds of mental cruelty and mental disorder under Section 13(1)(ia) and (iii) HMA. The parties lived together for less than a month in 2011 and remained separated for over 13 years with multiple criminal cases. High Court dismissed the divorce petition.
legal_issues: Whether continuous separation for 13 years with multiple criminal complaints constitutes mental cruelty under Section 13(1)(ia) HMA.
Exercise of Article 142 to grant divorce on irretrievable breakdown with permanent alimony.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. Decree of divorce granted dissolving the marriage under Article 142; husband directed to pay Rs. 35 Lakhs as permanent alimony to the wife.
legal_principles: Where spouses have stayed apart for more than a decade and all mediation attempts have failed, retaining the empty shell of marriage constitutes mental cruelty. Article 142 enables the court to dissolve the union with comprehensive financial security.
relevance_reason: Directly dissolves marriage under HMA and Article 142 on grounds of cruelty and irretrievable breakdown and awards permanent alimony.

case_name: Rina Kumari @ Rina Devi @ Reena v. Dinesh Kumar Mahto @ Dinesh Kumar Mahato and another
facts_summary: Husband obtained an ex-parte decree for restitution of conjugal rights under Section 9 HMA against his wife. When the wife sought maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, the husband contended that the restitution decree conclusively proved that she was living separately without sufficient cause, disentitling her to maintenance under Section 125(4) CrPC. High Court accepted husband's plea.
legal_issues: Whether an ex-parte decree for restitution of conjugal rights under Section 9 HMA operates as an automatic disqualification barring a wife from claiming maintenance under Section 125(4) CrPC.
Interplay between Section 9 HMA and Section 125 CrPC.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. High Court order set aside; maintenance under Section 125 CrPC restored.
legal_principles: A decree for restitution of conjugal rights under Section 9 HMA, especially an ex-parte decree, does not operate as an absolute legal bar against the wife claiming maintenance under Section 125 CrPC. The magistrate must independently determine whether the wife has just and sufficient reasons for living separately (such as neglect, ill-treatment, or cruelty).
sub_case_type: Maintenance & Restitution of Conjugal Rights (s.125 CrPC & s.9 HMA)
relevance_reason: Landmark decision harmonizing Section 9 HMA and Section 125(4) CrPC regarding maintenance rights despite a decree of restitution of conjugal rights.

case_name: Arathy Ramachandran v. Bijay Raj Menon
facts_summary: In a bitter child custody dispute, the High Court granted 15 days interim custody of minor school-going children to the father during term time. The mother appealed, contending that the order seriously disrupted the children's schooling and emotional stability.
legal_issues: Sustainability of interim custody orders under Guardians and Wards Act disrupting schooling and psychological stability of minor children.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. High Court's 15-day interim custody order set aside; visitation structured without disrupting school routine.
legal_principles: Interim custody under GWA must be tailored to ensure minimum upheaval in the child's academic and emotional routine. Extended physical transfers during term time should be avoided.
relevance_reason: Core child custody decision under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 regarding parameters for interim custody.

case_name: Saroj Salkan v. Huma Singh & Ors.
facts_summary: Appellant-daughter filed a partition suit under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 claiming coparcenary share in ancestral family properties. Single Judge of High Court dismissed the partition suit on admissions under Order XII Rule 6 CPC on its own motion without formal application.
legal_issues: Whether a partition suit claiming coparcenary rights under Section 6 HSA can be dismissed suo motu under Order XII Rule 6 CPC without full trial on disputed questions of joint family nucleus and partition.
decision_holding: Appeal dismissed on merits upholding the finding that properties had ceased to be coparcenary assets.
legal_principles: Judgment on admissions under Order XII Rule 6 CPC can be exercised where clear and unambiguous admissions demonstrate that properties are not joint family assets capable of partition under Section 6 HSA.
relevance_reason: Directly adjudicates partition claims and coparcenary status under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.

case_name: Rajesh Chaddha v. State of Uttar Pradesh
facts_summary: Husband was convicted under Section 498A IPC and Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act based on allegations of mental cruelty and dowry demands. High Court upheld conviction in revision.
legal_issues: What constitutes 'cruelty' under Section 498A IPC vis-à-vis ordinary domestic discord and incompatibility.
Whether vague and uncorroborated allegations of dowry demand justify criminal conviction under Section 498A.
decision_holding: Appeals allowed. Conviction under Section 498A IPC and Section 4 DP Act set aside; appellant acquitted.
legal_principles: Cruelty under Section 498A IPC requires conduct of such gravity as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or cause grave injury. Normal domestic friction, wear-and-tear of married life, or incompatibility do not attract criminal penal liability under Section 498A.
relevance_reason: Directly interprets the concept of matrimonial cruelty under Section 498A IPC in contrast to ordinary marital discord.

case_name: Shaurabh Kumar Tripathi v. Vidhi Rawal
candidate_laws: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
facts_summary: Reference on whether High Courts have inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC (or Section 528 BNSS) to quash complaints and proceedings initiated under Section 12 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.
legal_issues: Whether proceedings under Section 12 of the PWDVA are civil or quasi-criminal in nature.
Whether High Courts can invoke inherent powers under Section 482 CrPC to quash Section 12 PWDVA applications to prevent abuse of the process of court.
decision_holding: Appeals allowed. Supreme Court held that High Courts have full inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC / Section 528 BNSS to quash proceedings under Section 12 PWDVA.
legal_principles: Although PWDVA provides civil reliefs, the procedure before the Magistrate is governed by the CrPC and penal consequences arise under Section 31. Therefore, High Courts possess inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC to quash frivolous or malicious applications under Section 12 PWDVA to prevent abuse of judicial process.
sub_case_type: Domestic Violence / Quashing under Section 482 CrPC (s.12 PWDVA)
relevance_reason: Landmark decision authoritatively resolving the maintainability of Section 482 CrPC quashing petitions against applications under Section 12 of PWDVA.

case_name: Smt. Shaifali Gupta v. Smt. Vidya Devi Gupta & Ors.
facts_summary: In a family partition suit claiming shares in family properties, an application under Order VII Rule 11 CPC was filed seeking rejection of the plaint on the ground that the suit was barred under Section 4 of the Benami Transactions Act.
legal_issues: Whether a family partition suit can be rejected at the threshold under Order VII Rule 11 CPC on the ground that properties were purchased benami in the name of female family members.
decision_holding: Special Leave Petitions dismissed. Rejection of plaint refused; suit directed to proceed to trial.
legal_principles: Whether a property held in the name of a coparcener or female family member is joint family property or barred by the Benami Act is a mixed question of fact and law requiring trial, and cannot be summarily rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC.
relevance_reason: Deals with rejection of plaint in a family partition suit involving Hindu succession and joint family property claims.

case_name: In Re: Right To Privacy of Adolescents
facts_summary: Follow-up proceedings in In Re: Right to Privacy of Adolescents examining comprehensive policy and sentencing guidelines for cases of adolescent consensual sexual relationships and early marriages under POCSO and PCMA.
legal_issues: Sentencing discretion in POCSO cases involving adolescent consensual relationships.
Rehabilitation of minor victims and institutional safeguards under child protection and child marriage prevention laws.
decision_holding: Directions issued for victim rehabilitation, adolescent health education, and restorative sentencing approaches.
legal_principles: While the statutory mandate of POCSO and PCMA cannot be compromised, criminal sentencing must adopt restorative principles to safeguard the future of adolescents in consensual relationships without traumatizing victims.
relevance_reason: Examines intersection between child marriage prohibition under PCMA, adolescent sexuality, and POCSO sentencing.

case_name: Rakhi Sadhukhan v. Raja Sadhukhan
facts_summary: Wife challenged the quantum of permanent alimony fixed by the High Court at Rs. 20,000/- per month (with a 5% increase every three years) upon dissolution of marriage, pointing out husband's undisclosed high business income and luxury assets.
legal_issues: Quantum and enhancement of permanent alimony under Section 25 HMA.
Duty of full financial disclosure and assessing maintenance based on lifestyle and standard of living.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. Permanent alimony enhanced to Rs. 50,000/- per month with 5% increase every three years.
legal_principles: Under Section 25 HMA, permanent alimony must reflect the husband's real earning capacity and assets. Where income disclosures are suppressed, the court must draw realistic inferences from spending patterns and assets to secure dignity for the wife.
relevance_reason: Directly adjudicates permanent alimony enhancement under Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.

case_name: Vibhor Garg v. Neha
facts_summary: In divorce proceedings under Section 13 HMA, the husband sought to produce secretly recorded telephonic conversations with his wife as evidence to substantiate cruelty. High Court held the recordings admissible under Section 14 of the Family Courts Act.
legal_issues: Whether secretly recorded telephonic conversations between spouses can be admitted into evidence in divorce proceedings before the Family Court.
Whether admission of secretly recorded spousal conversations violates marital communication privilege under Section 122 Evidence Act and the fundamental right to privacy under Article 21.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. High Court order set aside; secretly recorded telephonic conversations held inadmissible in evidence.
legal_principles: Section 14 of the Family Courts Act does not permit reception of evidence obtained in flagrant violation of the fundamental right to privacy under Article 21 and privileged spousal communications under Section 122 Evidence Act. Secretly wiretapping a spouse's conversations without consent is an invasion of privacy and cannot be admitted to prove matrimonial cruelty.
sub_case_type: Divorce / Spousal Privilege & Wiretapping Evidence (Family Courts Act)
relevance_reason: Landmark decision on evidentiary admissibility, privacy, and spousal privilege under the Family Courts Act, 1984 and Section 122 Evidence Act in divorce proceedings.

case_name: Pradeep Bhardwaj v. Priya
facts_summary: Husband filed for divorce under Section 13(1)(ia) HMA. Spouses lived apart for nearly a decade with intense bitterness and failed conciliations. High Court dismissed the divorce appeal. Husband appealed to the Supreme Court seeking divorce under Article 142.
legal_issues: Whether the Supreme Court should dissolve a dead marriage under Article 142 on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage.
Provision of enhanced maintenance and permanent alimony for the wife and minor child.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. Decree of divorce granted under Article 142; child maintenance enhanced to Rs. 15,000/- per month and permanent alimony secured.
legal_principles: When emotional ties are shattered beyond redemption and living together is impossible, granting divorce under Article 142 is in the best interest of both parties and their minor child, provided full financial security is awarded.
relevance_reason: Directly dissolves marriage and enhances maintenance under HMA and Article 142 on the ground of irretrievable breakdown.

case_name: Ram Charan & Ors. v. Sukhram & Ors.
facts_summary: Legal heirs of a deceased tribal woman filed a suit for declaration of title and equal share in ancestral agricultural property. The claim was resisted on the ground that under Section 2(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, members of Scheduled Tribes are excluded from the Act, and customary tribal law denies inheritance rights to females.
legal_issues: Whether tribal women and their legal heirs are entitled to equal inheritance in ancestral properties despite the statutory exclusion in Section 2(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956.
Application of constitutional principles of justice, equity, and good conscience to eliminate gender discrimination in tribal succession.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. The Supreme Court held that tribal women are entitled to equal shares in ancestral property on principles of justice, equity, and good conscience.
legal_principles: Although Section 2(2) HSA excludes Scheduled Tribes from the statutory scheme, customary laws that disentitle women from inheritance solely based on gender violate Articles 14 and 21. Courts must apply the principles of justice, equity, and good conscience to grant equal succession rights to female tribal heirs.
sub_case_type: Succession & Inheritance / Tribal Women's Rights (s.2(2) HSA)
relevance_reason: Landmark judgment interpreting Section 2(2) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 and granting equal inheritance rights to tribal women.

case_name: Dasari Anil Kumar & Another v. The Child Welfare Project Director & Others
facts_summary: Appellants had taken minor children in informal adoption and nurtured them as their own children for years. Child Welfare authorities intervened to remove the children alleging lack of compliance with CARA / JJ Act adoption formalities, placing them in childcare institutions.
legal_issues: Whether custody of minor children should be retained with de facto adoptive parents who have raised them lovingly, or handed over to state institutions for technical procedural non-compliance.
Paramountcy of the 'best interest of the child' principle under Section 3 JJ Act and Article 142.
decision_holding: Appeals disposed of. Supreme Court directed custody to be returned to the adoptive parents, exercising Article 142 to regularize the adoption under JJ Act and HAMA principles.
legal_principles: Procedural formalities under adoption laws cannot override the paramount principle of the best interest of the child. Uprooting children from adoptive parents with whom strong psychological bonds exist causes irreparable harm.
sub_case_type: Adoption & Custody / Best Interest of Child (JJ Act & HAMA)
relevance_reason: Directly adjudicates child adoption and custody rights under HAMA, JJ Act, and Article 142.

case_name: A. Ranjithkumar v. E. Kavitha
facts_summary: Husband filed for divorce on grounds of mental cruelty and desertion under Section 13(1)(ia) and (ib) HMA. The Family Court granted divorce noting false police complaints and deliberate abandonment. High Court reversed the decree.
legal_issues: Whether leveling unfounded, defamatory criminal complaints and refusing cohabitation for over a decade amounts to mental cruelty under Section 13(1)(ia) HMA.
Correctness of High Court reversing Family Court findings.
decision_holding: Appeal allowed. High Court order set aside; decree of divorce granted by the Family Court restored.
legal_principles: Unfounded criminal complaints that cause public humiliation, combined with long years of desertion, constitute grave mental cruelty under Section 13(1)(ia) HMA. An appellate court should not overturn findings of cruelty where matrimonial trust is completely destroyed.
relevance_reason: Core matrimonial adjudication under Section 13(1)(ia) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 granting divorce for mental cruelty.

case_name: Madduri Gangaraju @ Babu Rao v. Madduri Sunanda & Others
candidate_laws: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
facts_summary: Subsequent to dissolution of marriage by a decree of divorce that attained finality and an amicable compromise settling all claims, the ex-wife filed fresh criminal proceedings under Sections 494 and 498A IPC and domestic violence claims against her former in-laws.
legal_issues: Whether criminal complaints under Section 498A and bigamy under Section 494 IPC can be maintained by an ex-wife against former in-laws after final decree of divorce and settlement.
Quashing of post-divorce vexatious criminal and DV proceedings under Section 482 CrPC and Article 142.
decision_holding: Appeals allowed. Criminal proceedings and FIRs against former in-laws quashed under Section 482 CrPC and Article 142.
legal_principles: Once marriage is dissolved by a decree of divorce and all matrimonial claims are settled, initiating criminal proceedings under Section 498A IPC or bigamy against former in-laws is a gross abuse of the process of law that must be quashed.
relevance_reason: Quashing of criminal and domestic violence proceedings instituted post-divorce decree, interpreting Section 482 CrPC and Article 142.

case_name: M.V. Leelavathi v. Dr. C.R. Swamy @ Dr. C.R. Kumara Swamy
facts_summary: Family Court granted a decree of divorce to the husband and awarded Rs. 15,00,000/- as permanent alimony to the wife under Section 25 HMA, which was affirmed by the High Court. The wife appealed to the Supreme Court seeking enhancement of permanent alimony pointing to the husband's lucrative medical practice and assets.
legal_issues: Assessment and adequacy of permanent alimony under Section 25 HMA commensurate with husband's high professional status and income as a doctor.
decision_holding: Appeals partly allowed. Decree of divorce affirmed; permanent alimony enhanced from Rs. 15 Lakhs to Rs. 40 Lakhs.
legal_principles: Permanent alimony under Section 25 HMA must ensure that the wife is not reduced to penury and can maintain a dignified lifestyle commensurate with the status she enjoyed during marriage. The earning capacity, professional qualifications, and assets of the husband are critical determinants.
relevance_reason: Directly adjudicates permanent alimony assessment and enhancement under Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
